CERVICAL & BREAST CANCER — BASIC AWARENESS
Warning Signs and the Importance of Regular Screening
Overview
Cervical cancer and breast cancer are two of the most common cancers affecting women in India, including in Odisha. Both are treatable when found early, and cervical cancer in particular can often be prevented altogether through vaccination and screening. Many women delay seeking care because of fear, embarrassment, lack of awareness, or limited access to health facilities near their homes. This document shares general awareness information — not a diagnosis — to help women and families recognise when a check-up is worth seeking, and to encourage regular screening as a normal, routine part of health care rather than something to fear or feel ashamed of.
Key Facts
Breast cancer and cervical cancer together account for a large share of all cancers diagnosed in Indian women, and are among the leading causes of cancer-related illness in the country.
Cervical cancer develops slowly, usually over many years, and is strongly linked to persistent infection with certain strains of the human papillomavirus (HPV). This slow progression is what makes screening so effective — it can catch changes long before cancer develops.
Breast cancer can affect women of any age but becomes more common with increasing age, particularly after 40 years, though it is increasingly seen in younger women too.
Government guidance recommends that women above 30 years of age be included in periodic screening for both breast and cervical cancer, even without any symptoms, as part of routine preventive health check-ups.
Screening tests for cervical cancer (such as visual inspection or Pap testing) and clinical breast examination are typically available free of cost through government health facilities, including Community Health Centres and District Hospitals, under national non-communicable disease control programmes.
Early detection significantly improves treatment outcomes and survival for both cancers, while late-stage diagnosis is associated with more difficult and costly treatment.
Common Concerns
Many women notice certain changes in their bodies but hesitate to mention them, assuming they will pass, or feeling too shy to discuss them, even with family or a doctor. Awareness of the following general changes can help someone decide when to consult a health worker or doctor. Noticing one of these signs does not mean a person has cancer — many are caused by other common, treatable conditions — but they should not be ignored.
Possible changes related to breast health include:
A new lump or unusual thickening in the breast or underarm area that does not go away.
Changes in the size, shape, or appearance of a breast.
Dimpling, puckering, or unusual texture of the skin over the breast.
Changes to the nipple, such as unusual discharge, redness, scaling, or the nipple turning inward.
Persistent pain in one specific area of the breast that does not follow the usual monthly cycle.
Possible changes related to cervical and reproductive health include:
Unusual vaginal bleeding — between periods, after menopause, or after intercourse.
Vaginal discharge that is unusual in colour, smell, or amount.
Persistent pelvic pain or discomfort, particularly during intercourse.
These signs are common early indicators referenced in general public health guidance, but only a qualified doctor can properly assess and interpret them.
When to Seek Medical Advice
A woman should consult a doctor or visit her nearest health facility if she notices any of the changes above, especially if they persist for more than two to three weeks or keep recurring. It is also important to attend screening even without symptoms, since both cervical and breast cancer can develop silently in the early stages before any noticeable changes occur. Women above 30 years of age are generally encouraged to have periodic screening as part of routine health care, regardless of whether anything feels wrong. Seeking care early is not something to be anxious about — most changes turn out to have simple, treatable causes, and a timely check-up is the best way to find out.
Odisha-Specific Context
Odisha's public health system, through the National Health Mission and the state's Non-Communicable Disease (NCD) control programme, offers screening for breast, cervical, and oral cancers at NCD clinics located in Community Health Centres and District Hospitals across the state. These services are intended to be free of cost and are aimed at reaching women in both rural and semi-urban areas, where distance, transport difficulties, and limited awareness have traditionally kept screening rates low. Anganwadi workers, ASHA workers, and auxiliary nurse midwives (ANMs) at the village level can guide women toward their nearest screening facility and help address common hesitations. Speaking with a local ASHA worker or visiting the nearest sub-centre is often the simplest first step toward getting screened.
Source Basis
This content is based on general, publicly available guidance from recognised health authorities, paraphrased and adapted for awareness purposes. It does not quote any source directly and is not intended to diagnose or guide treatment decisions. Reference sources consulted:
World Health Organization (WHO) — general guidance on cervical cancer and breast cancer prevention, early detection, and screening
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India — Operational Guidelines on Prevention, Screening and Control of Common Non-Communicable Diseases (NPCDCS), covering breast, cervical, and oral cancer
National Health Mission (NHM), India, and National Health Mission, Odisha — cancer screening programme framework and NCD clinic services
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) — published research on breast and cervical cancer burden and screening in India
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
